newsitem.title: USA: Nationwide may sell stake in unit in IPO - source.
newsitem.headline: Nationwide may sell stake in unit in IPO - source.

text.p: Nationwide Insurance Enteprise is considering a possible sale of a minority stake in its life insurance unit through an initial public offering, a source familiar with the situation said.
The move would help Nationwide raise capital to fund the expansion of its fast-growing life insurance business, industry sources said.

The Columbus, Ohio insurer has been working with investment bankers on a plan to sell about a 20 percent stake in the business to the public, but a decision has not been made whether to go ahead with the plan, the source said.
Nationwide is the fifth largest property-casualty insurer in the U.S. and ranks fourth in sales of variable annuity contracts, according to the company's annual report.

In the past five years, annuity and pension assets under management have increased nearly 136 percent to $33.5 billion from $14.2 billion. Nationwide's life insurance business had total assets of nearly $36 billion in 1995.
As a mutual insurance company, Nationwide is owned by its policyholders and therefore does not have access to the public equity markets.

"What a number of insurance holding companies are looking to do is find ways to capitalize on their growth subsidiaries," said Mark Puccia, director of insurance rating services for Standard & Poor's.
"Traditionally they have simply just downstreamed capital from the parent to the subsidiary," he said.
But some are "looking for ways to tap the public markets to get some of those capital needs," he said.
"It's a drain to do it continuously from the parent, especially in the context of a mutual, where a mutual has limited capital alternatives," he said.
A number of other insurance organizations with fast-growing subsidiaries are also considering initial public offerings, Puccia said.
"I'm seeing a lot of life companies being considered as IPOs," he said. "Life companies are real capital consumers."
These insurers are now weighing the strategic advantages of such a move, but the possible IPOs would not take place until the spring of 1997 at the earliest, Puccia said.
But the possible moves reflect some of the changes underway in the life insurance industry.
Many insurers are finding that they must commit additional capital to their life insurance businesses if they want to compete and some are not sure they want to do it.
Just last week, Chubb Corp said it was considering a possible sale or spinoff of its life insurance unit.
Chubb said that the additional commitment needed to make the mid-sized business competitive with its larger rivals may not be in the best interest of its shareholders.
